PAGE OFFSET RECORDED: Moran 2018 is printed = PDF + 66, verified at printed 77-79; Overlaet 2015 is a 278-page scan of the whole volume with the chapter at printed 138-157, printed = PDF - 18.

The Court Beguinages were 'incredibly stable, with most surviving religious upheaval and warfare to function well into the nineteenth century' (Moran 68 n.2), against the smaller communities which 'were far more transient'. Overlaet supplies the hard case: in 1578 the Mechelen city magistrate BURNED THE ENTIRE BEGUINAGE DOWN to deny shelter to a besieging force; after 1585 'most beguines returned and settled in a smaller beguinage within the city walls', bought houses and founded a new firmerie, and the community 'thrive[d] well into the twentieth century' (139, 152). An institution that survives the destruction of its entire physical plant and the dispersal of its members persists across their exit by any reading.
Founded in the thirteenth century and functioning into the nineteenth; no term, no single venture. Unproblematic, and it is one of the few cells here that needs no scoping.

Whether the institution was dissolvable or unwindable at will by a party is not addressed. The adjacent fact - that beguines made 'simple (non-permanent) vows' and could leave (Moran 68) - is about the member's tie, not about the arrangement, whose locator this characteristic gives as 'arrangement'. Coding the member's exit here would answer a different question, in the shape of the AP3/CF2 conflation the 2026-08-18 repair exists to prevent.

SCOPED TO THE POST-1585 POSITION AND LOW FOR THAT REASON. After the reestablishment of Spanish rule the bishops 'claimed the authority to rewrite and amend Beguinage statutes, to conduct visitations... and to intervene in issues concerning religious practice and community governance, which in turn shifted the Beguines' relationship to the ecclesiastical hierarchy by standardizing it and DECREASING THE BEGUINAGES' RELATIVE AUTONOMY' (80); the Mechelen statutes of 1588 were promulgated by archbishop Hauchinus (Moran 69 n.5). Amendment power lay outside the entity. MORAN PRESENTS THIS AS A CHANGE, and the medieval position is not established by anything read - Voigt 2012, 443 says the beguine way of life followed no supra-regionally binding rule and stood under no superior instance competent in matters of law and form of life, which if anything suggests the opposite value earlier. THIS CELL IS THE SECOND PIECE OF EVIDENCE FOR SPLITTING THE TYPE AT 1585; see the adjudications. .NR is the defensible alternative.

EXPLICIT AND UNUSUALLY WELL EVIDENCED. 'The Court Beguinages were internally divided into a standardized set of sub-institutions, each of which was financially independent from the others; these were the hof or court, the infirmary, the church, and the Table of the Holy Ghost... The hof acted as an umbrella institution in terms of discipline and administrative decisions BUT NOT FINANCIALLY' (77). Below those four, the konventen, the choir, each confraternity and each individual altar also kept their own funds and asset lists (79, 88), and 'separate account books were then drawn up for each sub-institution' (88). Joins isqa, nakai_fictive_household and the two ortoq rows on this value, and separates the form from every other corporate row in the matrix - casa_san_giorgio, the maone, the voc phases and bazacle_mill are all 'common'.

HALF-PRESENT ON ITS FACE AND THE TWO HALVES ARE SEPARATELY ATTESTED. Overlaet 144: 'According to its oldest (thirteenth century) and later ordinances (1588), all immovable property of beguines came into possession of the Great Beguinage of St Catherine. They were also expected to bring their own household furniture, goods and clothes, but THEY RETAINED OWNERSHIP OF THEIR MOVABLE PROPERTY, and were supposed to earn a living independently.' Immovables locked in, movables not. ARTICULATED VIA THE CANON LAW: Cum de quibusdam (1317) grounds its prohibition partly on the fact that beguines had taken no vow of obedience and had not renounced their property, and its saving clause exempts women living 'honeste in suis conversantes hospitiis' - in their own dwellings (Voigt 441). LOW, BECAUSE THE SOURCES PULL APART AND THE CELL RECORDS THE TENSION RATHER THAN RESOLVING IT: Moran has beguines managing personal property 'through the same legal channels as did everyday citizens' (79-80), owning annuities and 'properties and businesses located outside the Beguinages' (70), and the Antwerp profession book listing each postulant's retained annual passive income (70 n.8). Mechelen's ordinance may be local, or 'immovable property' may mean immovables within the hof. Put to the maintainer.

Two different interests and they differ. MEMBERSHIP IS NOT ALIENABLE: entry runs through the grand mistress's evaluation of the postulant (Moran 82), not through purchase from a leaver. THE HOUSING INTEREST IS PARTLY SO: what a beguine bought was 'a lifetime lease (lijfrent)' rather than the house (Moran 77 and n.16), which is personal to her and extinguishes at death - yet Overlaet 150 has Johanne De Bruyne bequeathing her nieces 'the lifelong usufruct of two rooms in Johanna's house' along with a share of her immovable property, so some transfer inside the community did occur by will. P records that split. Low: neither source asks whether a lijfrent could be assigned as such.

The opposite of depersonalised, and stated in terms. Kathelijne van Brecht's will left her niece Marieke a bed, furniture and clothing but 'explicitly linked these gifts to the condition that Marieke BECAME and remained a beguine herself' (138); the aunts' bequests were meant 'to provide their nieces with a dowry of sorts, one that would enable them to start their own beguine household'. The interest passes only to a named person who takes on the holder's identity - CI4 entails CI3, and this 0 sits consistently with CI3=P.

CF1 is 0, so the locator reverts to members. Nothing read establishes the extent or form of a beguine's liability for the institution's obligations to third parties; the liability discussed in Moran runs between sub-institutions (77) and between the institution and guilds (85-86), never to the members. See AP3 for why .NA was rejected.

The decision-makers are the mistresses. Whether they were exposed to the institution's outcomes - whether a shortfall on the hof's accounts touched the grand mistress in any way - is not addressed. Moran describes the accounting practice in detail (88-89: single-entry, income first, totals signed by the mistress and sometimes countersigned by the priest, audited by city-appointed rentmeesters) without ever saying what followed from a bad year. A striking silence given how much of the article is about money.

Returns are not shared proportionally to stake; the claim on the institution is a fixed provision, not a share. Beguines admitted to the infirmary or the poor table 'receive room and board... for the rest of their lives' - the same provision irrespective of what they brought, and in exchange 'they were required to sign over whatever remaining property they owned' (78). Everyone else pays rent or a lijfrent for a house and earns her own living. Joins waqf_khayri and ortoq_loan as the third 0 on this characteristic, and the waqf parallel is exact: an endowed corpus that provides rather than distributes.

MUTUALISATION OF MEMBER-SPECIFIC HAZARD, AND THIS IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL CELL IN THE BATCH. 'The infirmary and poor table together comprised a Court Beguinage's SOCIAL SAFETY NET, where Beguines who had become too poor to support themselves could be officially admitted as permanent charity cases and receive room and board (and at the infirmary, medical care if necessary) for the rest of their lives, but in exchange they were required to sign over whatever remaining property they owned' (78). Every element of pooling is present: a common fund (the infirmary held the largest portfolios, drawing 'the most pious donations'), contribution by members (bequests by beguines were a primary source of pachten and renten, 87, and the entrant signs over her residue), a hazard that varies across members (impoverishment, sickness, old age), and provision contingent on that hazard. CONTRAST partenrederij LR4=0 IN THE SAME BATCH, where the pooling is of capital into one hull and nothing member-specific is mutualised. MEDIUM, NOT HIGH, FOR TWO REASONS: Moran never frames it as insurance, and outside donations blur how far the fund is the members' own. See the adjudications - LR4 has variance at only two forms and a third 1 changes what the facet can support.

LR4 is 1, so the cell exists. The pooled baskets are individual beguines' economic fortunes, and impoverishment, illness and old age fall on members at different times - the infirmary carries a small standing group of dependants against a large paying membership, which is a diversifying structure. LOW, AND THE OBJECTION IS REAL: plague, war and a collapse in the textile trade hit the whole membership at once, and Overlaet 2015, 139 supplies exactly such a common shock - in 1578 the entire Mechelen community was dispersed and its houses burned. Moran does not address correlation at all, so this cell is an inference from the structure and would become synchronising, or .NR, on a different reading. Would be the second 'diversifying' in the matrix after nakai_fictive_household.
LR2 is .NR, so applicability cannot be settled and the direction of an exposure that has not been established cannot be recorded. .NA would assert LR2='veiled', which nothing supports.

The beguine's claim rests on being admitted to and remaining in the community: she is evaluated as a postulant, professes, is bound by statutes, elects the grand mistress, and can be expelled by her (Moran 77, 82, 83). Not a contract with a counterparty and not a beneficiary's claim on a corpus - which is what makes the waqf_khayri parallel at LR3 stop where it does. Overlaet 142 reports De Moor and Van Zanden reading beguinages alongside guilds as collectivities based on 'mutual agreement, which was not primarily kinship', and Lynch calling them 'artificial families'.

'The grand mistress, ELECTED BY HER COMMUNITY for a term of one to several years, was in charge of the assets held by the hof and wielded authority over the community as a whole' (77), and at Antwerp and Leuven several grand mistresses were elected together and divided the sub-institutions among themselves (83). MEDIUM RATHER THAN HIGH BECAUSE LEADERSHIP IS SHARED AND THE SHARE MOVED: she 'shared leadership with the Beguinage's priest' (77), and over the seventeenth century the bishops took the right to appoint that priest, so that where he had been 'an employee who could be fired' he became 'on equal or even higher footing than his community's grand mistress' (80-81). Collective still names the locus - the mistresses ran everything and were chosen by the members - but the qualification belongs on the record.

MG1 is 'membership', so the cell exists. Entry was screened, not open: the grand mistress evaluated postulants 'to ensure that they were of "good name and fame," properly pious, and CAPABLE OF FINANCIALLY SUPPORTING THEMSELVES' (Moran 82), and Overlaet's reading of the late sixteenth-century Mechelen ordinances is that 'only women of certain means were able to join the beguine community' (151), so that skills and capital were needed 'before they could even start thinking of becoming a beguine' (152). RESTRICTED BY QUALIFICATION, NOT BY NUMBER: no cap on membership is recorded anywhere, and Mechelen ran to 1,500-1,900 beguines (Overlaet 139). The characteristic reads 'closed OR numerically restricted', so 1 is right, but a reader wanting numerical closure specifically will not find it.

DECLINED FOR TWO INDEPENDENT REASONS, AND THE SECOND IS THE MORE INTERESTING. (i) NO FITTING VALUE. Moran 79: 'As liminal communities that straddled the conventional line between the laity and religieuses, the Court Beguinages HAD ALWAYS BEEN SUBJECT TO BOTH SECULAR AND ECCLESIASTICAL AUTHORITIES' - municipalities for taxation and building codes, city-appointed rentmeesters and momboren for audit and advice, bishops for statutes and visitation. MG4 asks for one answer and the source's answer is 'both, always'. Per the protocol, record .NR and flag rather than force the nearest wrong value. NOTE THAT partenrederij MG4 IS .NR IN THIS SAME BATCH for a structurally similar misfit - two of two forms. (ii) THE VALUE ALSO SPANS THE PERIOD. Medieval: Voigt 2012, 443 and 475 has a way of life that followed no supra-regionally binding rule, stood under no superior instance competent in law or form of life, and remained 'nicht approbiert' yet held in high standing; the communities themselves sought Schutzprivilegien from secular rulers, generally avoiding the term begina, and Count Robert of Flanders petitioned John XXII to modify Cum de quibusdam (473-474). Early modern: statutes promulgated by the archbishop (Moran 69 n.5, 80). 'customary' and 'religious' are both right for different centuries. Third piece of evidence for the split.

BOTH HALVES ARE ARTICULATED IN THE TRADITION'S OWN IDIOM, IN THE SAME STATUTES. Pious: the 1588 Mechelen preamble makes the beguinage 'voor alsulcke dochteren oft weduwen, die hun uyt des werels periculen begeren te trecken ende in maeghdelycke oft weduwelycke reynicheyt den Heere bequaemelijcke te dienen' (Moran 69 n.5). Mutual provision: the same 1588 ordinances require that all beguines 'sullen meesterlijck arbeyden een ieghelijck in haer handtwerck om haer broot te winnen' (Overlaet 149), and the institution runs an infirmary, a poor table, schools, a bakery and a brewery for its own members (Moran 78, 83-84). NOT commercial-profit: 'beguines were not expected to pursue profit: most beguinages put restrictions on the sale of their products' (Overlaet 150). THE ALTERNATIVE IS pious-charitable if FP1 is read strictly as the DECLARED purpose, which would align the row with waqf_khayri; mixed is coded because the provision half is declared in the same document, not inferred from practice.

A franchise held and defended as property, but not an exclusive one. The Beguinage bakery and brewery 'were exempt from the usual requirements to join the guilds and pay certain taxes and could thus provide bread and beer to community members for lower-than-market prices' (83-84), and the guilds litigated the privilege repeatedly - Diest butchers in the 1670s, the Leuven bakers in 1681, the Mechelen brewers for over half a century (85-86). That the privilege was worth half a century of litigation shows it was held as property. P rather than 1 because it is an exemption from guild and tax obligations, not an exclusive right to bake or brew: nobody else was excluded.

The form confers a status that is unavailable to its principals outside it, and the statutes say so. The 1588 preamble offers the beguinage to women who 'ben nochtans niet sterck genoech oft bequaem en gevoelen om eeuwege gelofften te doene, ende 't cloosterleven te aenveerden' - religious standing without perpetual vows (Moran 69 n.5). What the status carries with it is substantial: no vow of poverty and so retained movables and continued earning (Overlaet 144), personal property managed 'through the same legal channels as did everyday citizens' (Moran 79-80), and access to the guild-free bakery and brewery (FP2). CODED AS CONFERRAL, NOT AS MOTIVE, AND THE DISTINCTION MATTERS HERE: Overlaet's chapter tests the pragmatic reading and rejects it as the principal explanation - 'It seems highly unlikely, then, that the so-called great economic options beguines had can be viewed as the principal pull factor' (152), with the pious legacies in the wills showing 'religion played a far greater role in the lives of beguines than it did for lay single women' (148-149). This cell must not be read as endorsing piety-as-pretext.

Legible to political authority in both periods, by different routes. Early modern: 'For local and secular issues like taxation and building codes the Beguinages answered to their respective municipalities', and as institutions they 'answered to rentmeesters ("auditors") who were appointed to audit their accounts, while momboren ("guardians") functioned rather like a board of directors', both groups appointed by city authorities (Moran 79-80), with episcopal visitation on top. Medieval: after Cum de quibusdam the communities themselves applied to bishops and above all to secular rulers for Schutzprivilegien, and episcopal commissions in Cambrai, Tournai and Liege examined them under Cum de mulieribus (Voigt 473-474). ONE NUANCE WORTH KEEPING: Voigt notes those medieval privileges were obtained 'in der Regel unter Vermeidung des Terminus Begina' - legibility bought by not using the name.

The members are alike. Every beguine supports herself - the 1588 ordinances require each to work a craft to earn her bread - and 'all the positions, with the exception of the community's priest, chaplains, and a male advisory board, were filled by Beguines' (71). Those exceptions, and the masons, glaziers, brewers, gatekeepers, farmhands and laundry workers the mistresses hired (83-84), are employees on wages, not parties supplying labour to a capital-supplying counterparty. No capital-labour asymmetry inside the arrangement. THE VALUE SETS THE AP3/LR1 LOCATOR to members and makes CF2 inapplicable.

CF1 is 0: there is no labour-supplying party to the arrangement, so whether it bears loss of a principal's capital cannot be asked. Same disposition as asiento_averia, bazacle_mill, the maone, voc_1623 and waqf_khayri.

Approximately three dozen communities across the Southern Low Countries, Lille, Valenciennes, Breda and Amsterdam, ranging 'from just under a hundred Beguines to nearly a thousand' (71, 74); Mechelen ran to 1,500-1,900 (Overlaet 2015, 139). The largest membership of any form in this dataset.

The company could not own property. Legal title to the circulating trade assets was settled on a fixed body of trustees, and the shareholder-partners were equitable co-owners of the joint stock, no partner being able to claim any particular asset of the firm as his own (18, 37-38). The capacity that fails is capacity in the COMPANY, which had none; the trustee device is how the arrangement worked around that, and it is recorded here rather than coded. Entity locator as at LP1.

STRUCTURAL HALF, NOT A HEDGE, AND THE CELL A REVIEWER SHOULD LOOK AT FIRST. At common law the deed of settlement provided that the firm's litigation be conducted in the trustees' names alone, and this worked: the trustees held legal title to company property and to the debts owed the business and could sue on them in their own names 'without reference to the fluctuating body of shareholder-partners' (38; Metcalf v Bruin (1810), Lord Ellenborough CJKB). In Chancery it failed: joinder required every shareholder-partner as a party, Lord Eldon would not routinely dispense with it, and these companies 'could not reliably sue or be sued in Chancery' (50). Televantos's own summary is that 'a company could not sue in its own name, rather than that of its shareholders or trustees, without an Act of Parliament' (172). Read as the trustees the cell is 1; read as the company 0; read as the whole arrangement, which is what the 2026-08-31 locator rule requires, it is P. On the partners' bankruptcy the joint estate was administered as a distinct estate and distributed to partnership creditors in priority to each partner's separate creditors (22-23, 145; Ex p Ruffin (1801)). TELEVANTOS'S OWN EVIDENCE, NOT A RESTATEMENT OF HKS: the cell rests on Lord Eldon's judgments, the Bankruptcy Court order books (record class B 1) and Eldon's judicial notebooks. HKS is the frame he argues with, and at 144 he says in terms that Hansmann, Kraakman and Squire 'overlook limitations on partnership law's ability to preserve business assets for business creditors'. ARTICULATED on Lord Eldon's own words in Ex p Ruffin, quoted at 165: the joint creditors 'had clearly no lien whatsoever upon the partnership effects ... the equity is not that of the joint creditors, but that of the partners with regard to each other, that operates to the payment of the partnership debts'. THE PRIORITY IS DERIVATIVE AND DEFEASIBLE: it ran by subrogation to the partners' rights of indemnity and lien, so where the partners voluntarily discharged the lien by transferring the assets to a continuing partner the priority vanished - Ruffin's actual holding (166) - and 'Partnership creditors could thus never be safe from partners, by private agreement, emptying the partnership estate and so rendering their claims worthless' (168). That defeasibility is recorded here and NOT coded, because whether members can strip the pool is AP2's question.

Members' creditors: a separate creditor levying judgment against a partner's share could claim only that partner's right to the residue after the partnership creditors had been paid (148) - shielding present, and by a substantive rule. Members: as a matter of substantive law any partner could dissolve at will (24), which would partition the pool; in practice shareholders 'could not easily use the courts to dissolve or withdraw their capital from such concerns', and 'the difficulty shareholders had in suing such entities de facto acted as a capital lock-in mechanism' (51-52). Default partnership law dissolved the firm on any partner's death, retirement, bankruptcy, or simply at will, and even a new partner joining dissolved the old partnership and joint estate and created a new one (24, 150). Settling the assets on a fixed body of trustees was 'designed to insulate the company from the effect of the rules effecting mandatory partnership dissolution upon any change of partners, which could have been particularly troublesome in concerns with hundreds or even thousands of shareholder-partners' (38). It did not make the company persist as a legal unit - the courts treated these firms as partnerships throughout (43-46), and Chapter 7's Rule IV is that a single business in fact could in law be a succession of separate partnership estates (150) - but it did carry the asset-holding across the change of members. Half-present: the pool survives the member's exit, the entity does not. NOT CODED 1: Televantos nowhere says the device achieved succession. One common fund - the joint stock - vested in a fixed body of trustees who held the circulating partnership assets (37); the partners were equitable co-owners and 'no partner could claim any particular asset of the firm as his own' (18). The partners' 'separate estates' are their own patrimonies, not sub-pools of the entity, so nothing here engages the sub-pool exclusion. A partner's interest in the joint stock was residual. Each partner's right of indemnity was secured by an equitable lien over the others' shares, so no partner could claim any asset of the firm personally until the firm's creditors had been paid and an account taken (19-20), and a partner could not withdraw his stock from a factually insolvent firm because his share was then 'a liability rather than an asset' (147; West v Skipp (1749), quoted). For this form the effect was reinforced procedurally, shareholders being unable to use the courts to withdraw capital (51-52). CAUTION ON THE FRAME: Televantos cites Blair's 'locking in capital' only as part of the hindsight narrative he is criticising (28 n 91), and on his own account the lock-in here is a by-product of a jurisdictional refusal rather than a doctrine (51). Deed-of-settlement companies excluded the default partnership rule by providing expressly that partners could alienate their shares (36), and the trust made transfer effective by entry in the company's own books, operating as an assignment of the equitable interest by a direction to hold to the use of another (37; Ashby v Blackwell (1765)). TWO QUALIFICATIONS CARRIED, NOT RESOLVED: directors were typically given a veto over transfers (36 n 45); and free transferability was the very feature that exposed the company to prosecution under the Bubble Act until its repeal in 1825, and thereafter to Lord Eldon's view that raising sums by selling freely alienable shares without Act or Charter remained an offence at common law (40, 43, 172). Confidence medium for that reason: the clauses were drafted and used, their lawfulness was never settled.

Half-present. In form the interest was negotiable: shares changed hands by book entry (37) and were dealt in by stockbrokers - Josephs v Pebrer (1825) is a broker suing a client for unpaid shares (39) - amid a promotion boom that floated 624 companies in 1824-25 (39). In substance the holder's identity kept mattering: directors held a veto over transfers, every holder remained personally liable without limit, and Lord Eldon proposed a shareholder register precisely so that creditors could identify and sue them, with transfers null until registration (45). Televantos, following Ireland, dates the impersonal market in shares and the consequent separation of company from partnership to later in the century (44). CI4=P with CI3=1 is consistent with the declared entailment.

A coder persuaded by the contemporaries would code 'attenuated'; the legal fact codes 'coupled'. Confidence medium for that reason. Constituted by a private deed of settlement with no Royal Charter, patent or Act of Parliament, and that absence is the form's defining feature rather than an incident of it. It is also what made it precarious: the Bubble Act 1720 made it a criminal offence to purport to act as a corporation or to raise capital by issuing transferable stock without such authority (35), and after the Act's repeal in 1825 Lord Eldon held that doing so remained an offence at common law (43), saying in Van Sandau v Moore (1826) that the very 'inconvenience or impracticability of dealing with them in a court of justice, proved bodies of that kind to be illegal at common law' (50). Trading concerns: London corn factors, fire insurance companies, metal companies in Birmingham and the Midlands including Matthew Boulton's, and the Birmingham Flour and Bread Company (36), and the country banks whose collapses in 1810-11 and 1825-26 generate much of the litigation (150). Televantos's glossary defines the form as 'a business which raised capital by issuing shares and/or bonds' (183).

An observed absence, not a silence: the question is squarely put throughout. Corporate status and the privileges attached to it lay in the gift of Crown or Parliament and were granted to quasi-public entities such as canal companies and overseas trading companies (3); the deed-of-settlement company held no charter, patent or franchise; and Lord Eldon's objection to it was that raising large sums by selling freely transferable shares 'involved usurping privileges properly belonging to the Crown and Parliament' (40) - that is, holding none. SEPARATES FROM compagnie_antwerpen_1582, AND THE HALF IS THE POINT. The rule exists: 'la recopilacion de 1608 estipulaba por primera vez que los contratos de sociedad debian registrarse ante notario, y que cualquier reclamacion derivada de un contrato de sociedad escrito en privado se consideraba nula y sin efecto' (255). So from 1608 the society is in principle registered and legible to the municipal authority, which it was not before. The diffusion failed: the compendium 'no tuvo mucha influencia y el de 1582 siguio siendo el mas importante en la ciudad', its burdensome commercial formalities 'no se acogieron favorablemente', it was never printed, and its 3,643 articles made manuscript copying so laborious that circulation was obstructed (255). AGAINST THAT, AND WHY THIS IS P AND NOT 0: the Antwerp government did order the city court to apply the 1608 chapters on mercantile agreements (255), so the rule was not a dead letter but a poorly diffused one. A rule in force and badly circulated is half-present. Confidence medium, and a coder who weighted the failure of diffusion over the order to apply would code 0.
